triage.name: Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis
triage.reason: Left lower quadrant pain with fever and a clear CT-based diagnosis; strong acute abdomen differential including colitis and malignancy.

demographics: Diverticulosis is present in roughly one-third of US adults in their 50s and more than two-thirds of those over 80
Diverticulitis is somewhat more common in women in older age groups
More common in Western industrialized countries where low-fiber diets are typical
family_history: Diverticulitis or diverticulosis in a first-degree relative
social_history: Diet low in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains

chief_complaints.text: My lower belly hurts, mostly on the left side
I've had belly pain and a fever since yesterday
It hurts so much I can't get comfortable
I've been constipated and my belly is cramping

hpi.onset: Sudden in most attacks; in a minority the pain builds over one to several days
hpi.progression: Pain starts in the left lower abdomen and becomes constant and more intense; may localize and worsen with movement or coughing
hpi.location: Left lower quadrant, sometimes suprapubic or diffuse lower abdomen
hpi.radiation: May radiate to the back, groin, or suprapubic area; does not typically migrate
hpi.quality: Constant, aching or sharp; crampy in those with chronic diverticular symptoms
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe, often 6–8/10 during an acute attack

associated_symptoms.text: Urinary urgency or burning if the inflamed colon irritates the bladder

pertinent_negatives: Pain that started periumbilically and migrated to the right lower quadrant
Pain that started in the right lower quadrant
Profuse watery diarrhea with sick contacts
Weight loss or blood mixed in stool over weeks to months

argues_against: Painless bright red rectal bleeding as the only symptom suggests diverticular bleeding rather than diverticulitis
Chronic waxing and waning bloody diarrhea suggests inflammatory bowel disease
Flank pain with dysuria suggests pyelonephritis
Vaginal discharge suggests pelvic inflammatory disease
Missed period with one-sided pelvic pain suggests ectopic pregnancy
Purulent cervical discharge suggests pelvic inflammatory disease

negatives: Flank or back pain as the primary complaint
argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin suggests nephrolithiasis

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, weakness, or falls rather than prominent abdominal pain; fever and leukocytosis can be blunted.
May have minimal pain and fever despite perforation or abscess; a higher index of suspicion and lower threshold for imaging are needed.
Thick abdominal wall can make the exam less reliable; pain may be described as diffuse or poorly localized.
The colon is displaced upward by the enlarging uterus, so pain may be in the right lower or upper abdomen and mimic appendicitis or cholecystitis.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, no distress, afebrile-appearing
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, prefers to lie still, mild distress with movement
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, guarding the abdomen, reluctant to move
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, hypotensive, altered mental status, peritonitic

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the area of maximal pain
Ask the patient to cough, or tap the heel (gentler than releasing deep pressure)
findings.finding: Pain with jarring, suggesting peritoneal irritation

findings.maneuver: Deep palpate the left lower quadrant
findings.finding: Tender, ill-defined mass suggesting phlegmon or abscess

findings.maneuver: Auscultate bowel sounds in all quadrants
Auscultate bowel sounds in all quadrants

findings.finding: No mass, no gross blood, no tenderness
Anterior rectal tenderness or a palpable mass

findings.maneuver: Perform a pelvic exam when a gynecologic cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass

findings.maneuver: Examine the inguinal and femoral canals and any surgical scars for hernias

differential.name: Acute appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Acute onset abdominal pain with fever and leukocytosis; can present with right-sided or periumbilical pain that overlaps with atypical diverticulitis
differential.trigger: Pain that began periumbilically and migrated to the right lower quadrant, or right lower quadrant tenderness

history: Pain started centrally and migrated to the right lower quadrant
Anorexia with nausea before pain localizes
No prior similar left-sided episodes
exam: Maximal tenderness at McBurney point in the right lower quadrant
Psoas or obturator signs may be positive
imaging: CT shows an inflamed appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding and a normal sigmoid colon

differential.name: Acute colonic diverticular bleeding
differential.why_considered: Same underlying diverticula; patients may present with abdominal discomfort and rectal bleeding
differential.trigger: Large-volume painless bright red or maroon rectal bleeding

history: Painless, large-volume hematochezia
No fever or focal peritoneal pain
Often older adult on aspirin or NSAIDs
exam: Hemodynamically stable or tachycardic from blood loss; abdomen soft and nontender
labs: Falling hemoglobin with a normal or mildly elevated WBC
imaging: CT angiography or tagged RBC scan localizes the bleeding site; colonoscopy after stabilization shows diverticula without inflammation

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: Left-sided colon mass can cause abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and obstruction mimicking diverticulitis
differential.trigger: Weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, or persistent symptoms beyond the acute episode

history: Weeks to months of change in stool caliber
Unintentional weight loss
Blood mixed in stool
exam: Signs of anemia such as pallor
imaging: CT shows an irregular annular mass with luminal narrowing rather than diverticula with fat stranding

differential.name: Acute mesenteric ischemia
differential.why_considered: Severe abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting in an older adult with vascular risk factors
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to exam findings, or atrial fibrillation with sudden severe pain

history: Sudden severe pain that is poorly localized
Atrial fibrillation or known vascular disease
Pain much worse than the examination suggests
exam: Abdomen may be soft early despite severe pain
labs: Metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap
imaging: CT angiography shows arterial occlusion or bowel wall ischemia without the segmental colonic inflammation of diverticulitis

differential.name: Pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Fever, flank or abdominal pain, and leukocytosis can overlap with diverticulitis

history: Dysuria, urgency, and frequency preceding the pain
Flank pain radiating to the groin
exam: No focal left lower quadrant peritoneal signs
imaging: CT shows renal enlargement or perinephric stranding with a normal colon

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain with fever in a sexually active patient

history: Vaginal discharge
New or multiple sexual partners
Bilateral lower abdominal pain
imaging: Ultrasound shows thickened fallopian tubes or free pelvic fluid; CT shows no colonic diverticulitis

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Acute lower abdominal pain in a patient of reproductive age
differential.trigger: Any patient who could be pregnant with acute abdominal pain

history: Missed period
Vaginal bleeding
Sudden one-sided pelvic pain
imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine pregnancy and possibly an adnexal mass or free fluid

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic cramping, bloating, and altered bowel habits overlap with chronic diverticular symptoms

history: Chronic waxing and waning symptoms over months
Pain relieved by defecation
No fever or acute severe pain
imaging: CT or colonoscopy shows diverticula without inflammation

severity.mild: Uncomplicated diverticulitis: mild left lower quadrant pain, low-grade or no fever, able to tolerate oral intake, no peritoneal signs
severity.moderate: Uncomplicated diverticulitis with more marked pain, fever, leukocytosis, and guarding but no abscess or perforation
severity.severe: Complicated diverticulitis: abscess, phlegmon, fistula, obstruction, or contained perforation with significant systemic symptoms
severity.critical: Free perforation with generalized peritonitis and sepsis, or massive diverticular bleeding with hemodynamic instability

red_flags.meaning: Generalized peritonitis from free perforation; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe pain with hemodynamic collapse
red_flags.meaning: Free perforation or major diverticular bleeding

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status in an older adult
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or severe dehydration until proven otherwise
Abscess or perforation requiring drainage or surgery

complications.name: Fistula
clues: Pneumaturia or fecaluria suggesting colovesical fistula
Vaginal passage of stool or gas suggesting colovaginal fistula

complications.name: Stricture
clues: Narrowed segment on colonoscopy or imaging

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, weakness, or falls rather than prominent abdominal pain; fever and leukocytosis can be blunted, so a lower threshold for imaging is needed.
May have minimal pain and fever despite perforation or abscess; maintain a high index of suspicion and image early.

The enlarging uterus displaces the colon upward, so pain may be in the right lower or upper abdomen and mimic appendicitis or cholecystitis; CT is avoided when possible and ultrasound or MRI is preferred.
Thick abdominal wall can make the exam less reliable; pain may be diffuse or poorly localized, so imaging is essential.
Contrast-enhanced CT may need to be avoided; consider ultrasound or MRI, and adjust antibiotic dosing for kidney function.
May have atypical or blunted presentations and higher risk of severe complications; monitor glucose closely during acute illness.

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and how did it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant left lower quadrant pain that came on suddenly or built over a day or two

key_questions.question: When did the pain begin?
key_questions.looking_for: 12–72 hours; longer duration raises concern for abscess or perforation

key_questions.question: Does the pain move or radiate anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Stays in the left lower abdomen; may radiate to back or suprapubic area but does not migrate

key_questions.question: What makes the pain worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Walking, coughing, bearing down, or jarring the bed suggests peritoneal irritation

key_questions.question: Have you had fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills support inflammation or infection

key_questions.question: Any nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea common; vomiting suggests more severe disease or obstruction

key_questions.question: How have your bowel habits been?
key_questions.looking_for: Constipation common; diarrhea can occur; a change in stool caliber over weeks suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Have you seen blood in your stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Large-volume painless bleeding points to diverticular bleeding rather than diverticulitis

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, urinary frequency, or air in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Pneumaturia or fecaluria suggests a colovesical fistula

key_questions.question: Have you had episodes like this before, or been told you have diverticulosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior similar attacks or known diverticula support the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Have you had abdominal surgery or a colonoscopy?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior surgery suggests adhesions; recent colonoscopy may have shown diverticula

key_questions.question: Do you take ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, or steroids?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs and corticosteroids raise the risk of diverticulitis and bleeding

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had diverticulitis or diverticulosis?
Do you smoke, and how much physical activity do you get?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking and inactivity are modifiable risk factors

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes ectopic pregnancy in a patient of reproductive age

key_questions.question: Any vaginal discharge, bleeding, or pain with intercourse?
key_questions.looking_for: Present suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or a gynecologic cause

key_questions.question: Have you had unintentional weight loss or blood mixed in your stool over weeks to months?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests colorectal cancer rather than simple diverticulitis

key_questions.question: Any sudden severe pain with feeling faint, or large amounts of rectal bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Free perforation with peritonitis or major diverticular bleeding

reasoning_points: Constant left lower quadrant pain with fever and chills in an adult over 40
Tenderness and possibly guarding localized to the left lower quadrant
CT showing colonic diverticula with segmental wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding
Complications considered: abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction, and bleeding
Alternatives excluded: appendicitis, colorectal cancer, mesenteric ischemia, pyelonephritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy
NSAID or corticosteroid use noted as a risk factor

easy: Classic left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis
CT confirms sigmoid diverticulitis without complication
medium: Older adult with blunted pain and fever who presents with weakness or confusion
Mild symptoms with normal white count but CT shows diverticulitis
Woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain and gynecologic look-alikes
hard: Immunocompromised patient with minimal pain and fever despite abscess or perforation
Pregnant patient with right-sided or upper abdominal pain from a displaced colon
Patient presenting with pneumaturia or fecaluria from a colovesical fistula
Elderly patient with painless large-volume rectal bleeding from diverticular bleeding rather than diverticulitis
Presentation after free perforation with diffuse peritonitis and sepsis
